title: Preferences and consumer choice
review_type: Specialist author mathematical, instructional, computational and scoped primary-source review; root independently audits and alone accepts

reviewed.reasoning: Defined complete/transitive preferences, strict preference, indifference and ordinal utility before choice. The finite-set representation construction and lexicographic continuity counterexample do not claim a universal infinite-domain representation theorem. Distinguished continuity, convexity, strict convexity, quasiconcavity, concavity and local nonsatiation. Proved positive-price compact-budget existence, LNS budget exhaustion, degree-zero homogeneity, convex demand sets and strict-convexity uniqueness, with explicit convex-feasibility and attainment assumptions. Explained positive-price, zero-income, negative-income, free-good, satiation and integer-feasibility boundaries. Stated MRS units and derivative-zero transformation limits. Derived the maximizing KKT signs and constraint qualification, then proved global sufficiency under concavity rather than treating every tangency as sufficient.
reviewed.worked_examples: Three original complete cases: smooth x1^2*x2 demand via interiority and the strictly concave log representation; shifted-log demand via a strictly concave one-dimensional objective with both genuine corners and endpoint equalities; substitute demand correspondences versus fixed-proportion kink uniqueness. Smooth utility is not equated with interior choice, and unique choice is not equated with globally strictly convex preferences. Exact demands (15,5), (12,5), shifted-log (2,12)/(1,0)/(0,18), substitute budget segment and recipe (6,3) were independently recomputed.
reviewed.revealed_preference: Separated WARP for a fully observed maximizing correspondence, its distinct-choice unique-demand budget implication and the tie-permitting pairwise inequality under LNS. Proved each necessary implication using optimality/transitivity or the strict-budget-slack argument. The tied same-budget example passes the weaker condition, while the strict two-budget example fails it. A three-good, three-budget cycle passes all pairwise unique-demand tests but contradicts stable LNS maximization through a longer strict cycle. No finite-data rationalization sufficiency theorem is asserted. Empirical interpretation explicitly concerns the joint commodity, budget, stability, nonsatiation and optimization assumptions.
reviewed.solutions: Read all eight matched solutions and recomputed all determinate results: ordinal and expected-utility transformation counterexamples; the bliss-point demand with 5 USD slack; new exponents and shares; three shifted-log regimes and a ration; full continuous and integer substitute choices and a nonconvex feasibility counterexample; changed-price fixed recipe; strict two-budget contradiction versus equal-cost ties; and the pairwise-consistent three-cycle. Explanatory questions have explicit reasoning or evaluation criteria. The delayed check has exact interior and corner answers and the nominal-rescaling implication.
reviewed.instruction: The chapter states its capability, full prerequisite route, units, commodity period and original synthetic scope. It teaches every exercise method before use, integrates definition/proof/counterexample and economic interpretation, and ends with Teach-back and Delayed check. D(p,m) denotes the Marshallian correspondence and x(p,m) only a singleton-valued demand. It hands compensated choice, duality, Slutsky and welfare to c02 without assuming those methods here. No separate laboratory assets are needed for this mathematical chapter.
reviewed.sources: Retrieved actual scoped contents of two official Wolitzky MIT course PDFs and Bergstrom's author-hosted UCSB revealed-preference notes. Inspected preference/continuity/convexity/WARP sections, budget/existence/LNS/homogeneity/KKT sections, and tie/strict-affordability/chain distinctions. Source proposals record exact titles, URLs, uses, check date and inspection boundaries. Original examples, exercises, proofs and wording were composed for this chapter; no source exam or workbook exercise was copied. The Bergstrom record states a subsequent screenshot cache miss honestly; successful full-text retrieval underlies its inspection.
reviewed.structure: Balanced static HTML fragment, no h1, three aside.worked cases, eight ol.exercises items and eight corresponding main solution items in one details.solutions block, unique IDs, three matching cited source IDs, foundation assessment and successor routes. No shared manuscript, central acceptance, publishing or visual-QA action performed. Root independently read the full chapter and all eight solutions and requested no mathematical content correction.
